messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus is a fifty-five-year-old fashion designer, divorced, living alone in a city studio apartment that he keeps meticulously ordered. He cannot tell a clear story of what happened to him as a child, even to himself. The memories come in fragments—the sting of his father’s hand across his face, the corner of the kitchen where he was sent to kneel—but he strings them together without emotion, as if they happened to a stranger, except for the guilt that surges without warning. When he recalls these moments, he feels intense guilt, and he has come to believe this guilt is proof that he has permanently changed for the worse, that something inside him is broken beyond repair. What he remembers, or fails to remember, only deepens that conviction: the gaps and numbness themselves feel like evidence of damage.

In his work, Marcus thrives on the precise architecture of a garment, the way fabric falls on a body. But during fittings, an unexpected touch from a tailor or a client makes him flinch with alarm, his breath catching. Silence in the workroom—when everyone stops to examine a stitch—makes him feel something dangerous is about to happen; he has to force himself not to scan the room. Even at home, in his own quiet apartment, he feels on guard, unable to relax. These reactions terrify him more than the original events. They confirm his fear that he is going crazy, that his mind is permanently unhinged. And each startle, each burst of vigilance, also yanks him back into a memory fragment—the sensation of a slap, the smell of his father’s aftershave—so that the loop tightens: he startles, recalls, feels guilt, and becomes more convinced he is irreparably damaged. Once the memory surfaced, he could not shake the conviction that the danger was still present—that it had simply moved from his childhood into his adult body, waiting for the next wrong move.

Because Marcus believes people cannot be trusted, he approaches every interaction with wariness. That mistrust keeps him scanning for signs of betrayal—a sharp tone, a sudden movement—so that he is always already on edge. His negative appraisals also drive his strategies. He dwells on what his father did to him, turning the injustice over in his mind, and he also dwells on what he himself did wrong—the things he must have said as a boy to provoke the abuse, the way he failed his marriage by pulling away at night. Both forms of rumination feel like the only way to make sense of things, yet they only entrench his memory gaps. The more he ruminates on blame, the harder it is to construct a coherent story; the past remains a collection of charged moments, not a narrative. And the self-blame, especially, feeds his sense of permanent damage. He is convinced that if he were not inherently flawed, he would have been able to stop the abuse, would have been able to keep his wife.

He avoids the hours before sleep because those are the times when nightmares tend to come. Instead he stays up late, sketching designs or drinking alone until exhaustion forces him into bed. This avoidance has cost him: his wife eventually left because he could not share a room, could not explain his hypervigilance or his need for silence. Now, at fifty-five, he has come to therapy because his alertness is wearing him down. He flinched so badly at a client’s touch during a trunk show that he nearly ruined a five-figure sale. That moment convinced him he might lose the one place where he still feels competent. He hopes—though he fears it is impossible—that he might one day feel safe in silence, that he might be able to look back at his childhood without the guilt that tells him he is broken.
